title: Where to see the Northern Lights, from Tromsø to Caithness
excerpt: Where to see the Northern Lights this winter, from classic aurora destinations such as Tromsø and Abisko to quieter spots in Greenland, Finland and northern Scotland.

Where to see the Northern Lights this winter, from classic aurora destinations such as Tromsø and Abisko to quieter spots in Greenland, Finland and northern Scotland.

November 10, 2026 3-min read

Add as a preferred source on Google

For many travellers, the chance to see the Northern Lights ranks alongside the Great Migration in Africa, a trip to Antarctica or sunrise over Machu Picchu as one of life’s unforgettable moments. Photographs capture the colours, but rarely the feeling of standing under a sky filled with moving ribbons of green, purple and pink light.

Part of the aurora’s appeal is its unpredictability. Every display is different. Some nights bring a faint green shimmer on the horizon, while others erupt into curtains of colour across the whole sky. Travellers often spend hours wrapped up against the cold, waiting, and the anticipation becomes part of the experience.

The lights appear when charged particles from the sun collide with gases in the Earth’s atmosphere, creating displays around the polar regions. Indigenous cultures across the Arctic have long woven the lights into their folklore. The best viewing spots are usually far from towns, where dark skies reveal the aurora and a sky full of stars.

The classic places to see the Northern Lights

Tromsø, Norway

Often called the gateway to the Arctic, Tromsø combines good aurora viewing with restaurants, culture and outdoor activities, and its fjords and mountains make dramatic backdrops for photography.

Iceland

Iceland is one of the most accessible aurora destinations, with the lights visible above volcanic plains, black-sand beaches, waterfalls and glaciers. Reykjavik is a popular base, but the countryside offers much darker skies.

Finnish Lapland

Glass igloos, reindeer safaris, snowmobile trips and wilderness make Finnish Lapland a classic winter choice, and new hotels keep arriving, as we reported when the Arctic Boutique Collection expanded across Finnish Lapland.

Abisko, Sweden

Abisko National Park in Swedish Lapland is known for its microclimate, which often keeps skies clear when nearby areas are cloudy.

Yukon, Canada

With vast wilderness and little light pollution, Canada’s Yukon Territory offers some of North America’s best displays. Our feature on why the Yukon suits a winter coolcation has more.

Alaska, USA

Fairbanks is one of the world’s best-known aurora destinations, where visitors can combine the lights with dog sledding, hot springs and wilderness trips.

Hidden gems with smaller crowds

Some lesser-known places can offer equally memorable displays, often with fewer people around.

Murmansk region, Russia

The area around Murmansk, well inside the Arctic Circle, sees frequent aurora activity in winter. However, the UK government advises against all travel to Russia, and travel against that advice can invalidate insurance.

The Faroe Islands

Between Iceland and Norway, the Faroe Islands offer dramatic coastlines and dark skies. The weather is changeable, but patient visitors may see the lights above towering cliffs.

Raufarhöfn, Iceland

Far from Iceland’s busiest routes, this small fishing village in the north-east has exceptionally dark skies.

Kangerlussuaq, Greenland

One of Greenland’s most reliable aurora spots, Kangerlussuaq has a dry climate and frequent clear nights.

Salla, Finland

Often overshadowed by Lapland’s larger resorts, Salla offers forests, frozen lakes and little light pollution for a quieter trip.

Northern Scotland

Many travellers forget that the aurora can be seen from the UK. Shetland, Orkney, Caithness and parts of the Outer Hebrides regularly see displays strong enough to light up the northern sky.

Churchill, Manitoba, Canada

Best known for its polar bears, Churchill also sits beneath the auroral oval, making it one of Canada’s most underrated Arctic destinations.

Fitting an aurora trip around work

For business travellers heading to Oslo, Stockholm, Helsinki or Reykjavik in winter, a few extra days in the north can turn a work trip into a chance to see the Northern Lights. Displays cannot be guaranteed, so it is worth allowing several nights and booking tours with flexible cancellation.

What keeps the aurora at the top of so many wish lists is that it goes beyond sightseeing. No two displays are the same, and no camera fully captures the moment the sky comes alive.
